title: Identify motor types
summary: Tell brushed DC, universal, brushless, stepper, induction and synchronous motors apart by their wires, labels, shape and feel, and know which ones make good generators, pumps and drives.

steps.text: Start with the label: AC or DC, voltage, speed in rpm, and words like brushless, stepper, PMDC or capacitor run. A frequency in Hz means it runs on AC.

Count the wires. Two: brushed DC, universal, or a small AC or synchronous motor. Three thick wires: brushless (BLDC) or three-phase AC. Three thick wires plus five thin ones: brushless with Hall sensors. Four, five, six or eight similar thin wires: a stepper. Three wires and a capacitor nearby: single-phase AC.

Turn the shaft by hand with the leads apart. An even, regular notchy feel (cogging) means permanent magnets: brushed DC, brushless, stepper or synchronous. A smooth feel means an induction or universal motor.
Look for brushes: small square or round caps on the end of the motor, carbon dust inside, or a copper commutator with many segments. Brushes mean brushed DC or universal.

Brushed DC or universal? Spin it with the meter on DC volts. A magnet DC motor makes a clear voltage; a universal motor makes almost none. Universal motors have wound coils instead of magnets, run on mains, and scream at high speed in vacuums, blenders and power tools.

Brushless motors have three equal windings, magnets on the rotor and no brushes. They are in e-bike and scooter hub motors, hoverboards, drones, computer fans, direct-drive washers and newer cordless tools. They need a controller to run.
Steppers have square flanged bodies (often about 42 mm square in printers), four to eight wires, and a strong, crisp notchy feel. They need a driver board.

Induction motors are heavy and spin smoothly, often with a capacitor or a centrifugal switch inside. They are in washers, pumps, fans, compressors and workshop machines, and need AC at the right voltage and frequency.
Shaded-pole motors are small, cheap AC motors with a thick copper ring around part of the iron core. They run fans in microwaves, fridges and bathrooms. They are weak and can't be used as generators.
Synchronous motors are small sealed motors with a gearbox and a fixed slow speed, such as microwave turntable and timer motors. They have magnets and make a small AC voltage when you spin them.
steps.warn: When you open magnet motors, the rotor can snap back into the case. Keep fingers clear of the gap.

steps.text: Pick by job. Generators need permanent magnets: brushed DC, brushless or stepper. Pumps and fans run well on induction motors from AC. Carts, winches and drives want big magnet DC motors, or brushless motors with their controller.

notes:
## Quick reference

| Type | Wires | Brushes | Magnets | Runs on | Common sources | Best uses |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Brushed magnet DC | 2 | Yes | Yes | DC | Treadmills, wipers, drills, toys, car seats | Generators, DC drives, winches |
| Universal | 2 | Yes | No | AC or DC mains | Vacuums, blenders, corded tools | Fast mains tools and fans |
| Brushless (BLDC) | 3 thick (+5 thin) | No | Yes | DC through a controller | Hub motors, hoverboards, drones, direct-drive washers | Efficient drives, generators |
| Stepper | 4, 5, 6 or 8 | No | Yes | Pulses from a driver | Printers, 3D printers, scanners, optical drives | Precise positioning, small generators |
| Induction | 2–4 | No | No | AC | Washers, pumps, fans, compressors, machines | Long-running pumps and fans |
| Shaded-pole | 2 | No | No | AC | Small fans in microwaves and fridges | Small fans |
| Synchronous | 2 | No | Yes | AC | Microwave turntables, timers | Slow turntables, tiny generators |

## Generators

A motor with permanent magnets makes electricity when you turn it. The faster you turn it, the higher the voltage.

- Big brushed DC motors from treadmills make good wind and water generators.
- Brushless motors make three-phase AC; rectify it with diodes to charge batteries.
- Steppers make useful power at slow speeds for small loads.
- Induction and universal motors don't make useful power on their own.
- A car alternator has a wound rotor, not magnets: it needs a little battery current to start making power.

## Hall sensor wires

Brushless motors with sensors usually have five thin wires: a supply (often 5 V), ground, and three signal wires. Don't confuse them with the three thick phase wires, and don't put power on them.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming every three-wire motor is brushless. Single-phase AC motors often have three wires too.
- Connecting a brushless motor straight to a battery. It needs a controller.
- Running a 50 Hz motor on 60 Hz or the other way round without checking the label.
- Opening magnet motors without expecting the rotor to snap back in.
